sources.title: Screen Time & Temper Tantrums: Helpful Tips for Parents
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (by Jenny Radesky, MD, FAAP; last updated 3/13/2024)
sources.quote: Toddlers and younger school-aged children are still learning to deal with anger, frustration and disappointment. ... You can help build a bridge back to reality by entering the room or sitting down near your child, quietly observing what they're doing. When you see signs that they're willing to engage, offer a warm smile of encouragement. ... Try it with younger kids, too: offer a beloved book, cuddle time with the family pet or a small chore that makes them feel part of the group.
sources.supports: Young children are still learning to deal with frustration and disappointment; sitting near the child and quietly watching what they do helps them come back; for younger kids 'trading up' can offer a beloved book. Fragments read in the page today, joined with ' ... '.

sources.title: Two-minute warnings make kids’ ‘screen time’ tantrums worse
sources.publisher: UW News, University of Washington (Jennifer Langston, May 5, 2016; on Hiniker, Suh, Cao and Kientz, CHI 2016)
sources.quote: Some things did make that switch easier, like having routines, disengaging at a natural stopping point or simply having a battery die. But children aged 1 to 5 who were given a two-minute warning by their parents were more upset when the screen went away. ... Natural stopping points in the content children were viewing or in the games they were interacting with made transitions easier
sources.supports: Routines and a natural stopping point made the switch easier in a diary study of families with children aged 1 to 5. Fragments read in the page today, joined with ' ... '.

sources.title: How do I put a stop to screen time (turn off the TV or take the phone away) without causing a meltdown?
sources.publisher: Common Sense Media (the Child Mind Institute contributed; last reviewed or updated September 27, 2021)
sources.quote: Have a plan. Explain beforehand to your kid that he or she can watch a certain number of shows or for a specific time period. Let them know what to expect after the show, too. ... Show your kids how to turn off the TV. They may enjoy practicing that skill, and it will give them some power over their situation, which they'll appreciate. ... Give praise. If your child successfully transitions to another activity without a meltdown, show your appreciation. Say something like, "Thanks for turning off the TV and coming to set the table!" Kids will be more likely to follow through again when they have a positive experience.
sources.supports: Say beforehand how many shows and what comes after; show the child how to turn off the TV for some power over it; praise a calm switch with a sentence like 'Thanks for turning off the TV and coming to set the table!'. Fragments read in the page today, joined with ' ... '.

sources.title: 3 ways to help your child transition off screens and avoid the dreaded ‘tech tantrums’
sources.publisher: The Conversation (Juliana Zabatiero, Kate Highfield, Leon Straker and Susan Edwards; published January 9, 2024)
sources.quote: Some successful strategies parents and carers in this research used were “you can watch two episodes of this show” or “when this game is finished we will stop”. ... Telling them what activity would follow was also helpful. For example “when you have finished that game it will be time to eat” or “after you have watched that show we will go to the park”. What they are moving to may not always be fun, helping children understand what to expect helps make for a smoother transition. ... Parents reported success when providing kids with simple choices when preparing to move off technology. For example “would you like to watch two or four episodes of this show?” or “would you like to start the timer for your game or do you want me to let you know when your time is up?” ... For example if your child has been watching Bluey you could invite them to complete a Bluey puzzle, or role-play some Bluey games such as keepy uppy or obstacle course. ... Families in this study reported moving from watching Fireman Sam to visiting a fire station or building a fire station with their child using blocks and other play materials in the home.
sources.supports: Parents in a 12 week study found these helped: 'you can watch two episodes', saying what comes next, simple choices ('two or four episodes?') and a real-life game inspired by the show (a puzzle, building it with blocks). Fragments read in the page today, joined with ' ... '.

sources.quote: Parents reported that screen time transitions were easier when they were part of a routine. Parents also reported that features like “autoplay” — which automatically starts another video when one ends — or suggested videos that pop up and tempt children to keep watching were a frustrating and driving force behind many of their battles. ... Screen time transitions also went more smoothly if the technology was to blame. ... “The kids we looked at for this particular study are right in that power struggle age,” Kientz said. “It’s much easier to do that with a person than with technology. Once you take that parental withholding component out of it, kids are a lot more accepting.”

sources.title: Two-minute warnings make kids’ ‘screen time’ tantrums worse
sources.publisher: UW News, University of Washington (Jennifer Langston, May 5, 2016; on Hiniker, Suh, Cao and Kientz, CHI 2016)
sources.quote: Giving young children a two-minute warning that “screen time” is about to end makes transitions away from tablets, phones, televisions and other technological devices more painful, a new University of Washington study has found. ... Some things did make that switch easier, like having routines, disengaging at a natural stopping point or simply having a battery die. But children aged 1 to 5 who were given a two-minute warning by their parents were more upset when the screen went away. ... every way we sliced it, the two-minute warning made it worse. ... Parents also reported that features like “autoplay” — which automatically starts another video when one ends — or suggested videos that pop up and tempt children to keep watching were a frustrating and driving force behind many of their battles. ... Parents reported that screen time transitions were easier when they were part of a routine. The same child who might argue and negotiate for more screen time after a Friday night treat may be perfectly fine with turning off the TV when breakfast is ready if that is part of the daily household routine. ... “The kids we looked at for this particular study are right in that power struggle age,” Kientz said. “It’s much easier to do that with a person than with technology. Once you take that parental withholding component out of it, kids are a lot more accepting.”
sources.supports: In a diary study of families with children aged 1 to 5, a parent's two-minute warning made the end more painful ('every way we sliced it'); routines and natural stopping points helped; autoplay drove battles; the TV off when breakfast is ready as a routine; children of this age accept the end more easily from technology than from a person. sources.title: How do I put a stop to screen time (turn off the TV or take the phone away) without causing a meltdown?
sources.publisher: Common Sense Media (the Child Mind Institute contributed; last reviewed or updated September 27, 2021)
sources.quote: Avoid back-to-back shows. If you're using a streaming service, disable the setting that automatically plays the next show in a series. ... Create a routine. Kids who know they have to turn off the TV before a specific activity (like dinner) can sometimes transition more easily. ... Show your kids how to turn off the TV. They may enjoy practicing that skill, and it will give them some power over their situation, which they'll appreciate. ... Give praise. If your child successfully transitions to another activity without a meltdown, show your appreciation. Say something like, "Thanks for turning off the TV and coming to set the table!" Kids will be more likely to follow through again when they have a positive experience.

sources.publisher: The Conversation (Juliana Zabatiero, Kate Highfield, Leon Straker and Susan Edwards; published January 9, 2024)
sources.quote: We would be upset if we were watching a movie and someone suddenly stopped it midway through without warning. ... Just like adults, children can feel very annoyed and frustrated when their device is suddenly taken away, especially when they are enjoying a game or watching content they like. ... So you need to prepare children and let them know when their time with a screen will end. ... Some successful strategies parents and carers in this research used were “you can watch two episodes of this show” or “when this game is finished we will stop”. ... Telling them what activity would follow was also helpful. For example “when you have finished that game it will be time to eat” or “after you have watched that show we will go to the park”. What they are moving to may not always be fun, helping children understand what to expect helps make for a smoother transition.
sources.supports: The adult analogy (a movie stopped midway without warning), that children feel annoyed and frustrated when a device is suddenly taken away, preparing them for when screen time ends, 'when this game is finished we will stop', and saying what comes next even when it is less fun. Fragments read in the page today, joined with ' ... '.

sources.title: Screen Time & Temper Tantrums: Helpful Tips for Parents
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (by Jenny Radesky, MD, FAAP; last updated 3/13/2024)
sources.quote: Toddlers and preschoolers already know they can't eat ice cream at every meal or spend all their time playing with a single toy. A healthy life requires balance and variety. You can build on this concept when you talk about screen time. ... When kids have tantrums, parents need to avoid having one too. ... Pausing before speaking or acting can help you maintain the calm you need to help your child. ... researchers found that tossing a pillow in the air and challenging kids to bat it in a new direction helped work off momentary tension. ... You can help build a bridge back to reality by entering the room or sitting down near your child, quietly observing what they're doing. When you see signs that they're willing to engage, offer a warm smile of encouragement. ... Kids of all ages will resent limits that adults don't follow themselves. ... Try it with younger kids, too: offer a beloved book, cuddle time with the family pet or a small chore that makes them feel part of the group.
sources.supports: Talking about balance on a calm day (no ice cream at every meal); staying calm and pausing before answering; tossing a pillow to bat for physical acting out; a warm smile when the child is ready to engage; kids resent limits adults don't follow; a beloved book when trading up.
